materials.title: Expository Text and Analytical Exposition
materials.content:
## What is an expository text?

Expository text is a text that conveys fact and opinion about a topic. One form of expository text is analytical exposition. Analytical exposition is a text that elaborates the writer's idea about an issue. It adopts a position with respect to the issue that becomes the subject of the writing and provides evidence in support of that position. It aims to persuade the readers to adopt the position taken by the writer. It consists of a statement of position, arguments, and reiteration or conclusion.

### Structure

| Part | Function | Example from the graffiti texts |
|---|---|---|
| Statement of position | States the issue and the writer's view | Graffiti is art, and it is essential in our culture. |
| Arguments | Give reasons and evidence that support the position | First, graffiti enables the public to see something new. Second, it affects people positively. |
| Reiteration or conclusion | Restates the position and closes the text | Every person must strive to educate themselves of the origins of graffiti. |

### Language features

- The simple present tense states general claims: Graffiti is always vandalism.
- Connectives order the arguments: first, second, next, furthermore, the last reason.
- Conclusion markers signal the closing: thus, in conclusion, therefore.
- Evaluative words carry the writer's judgement: masterpiece, meaningless, crime, positivity.
- Modality shows obligation or certainty: must, should, would, can.
- Key terms are repeated so the issue stays in focus: graffiti, artist, vandalism, public.

### Words about art and graffiti

| Name | Description |
|---|---|
| Autograph | One's name as written by oneself |
| Tag | A writer's signature with spray paint or marker |
| Graffiti | Drawings or inscriptions made on a wall or other surface |
| Mural | A large picture painted on the wall |
| Scribble | To write hastily or carelessly |

An analytical exposition is judged by whether the arguments really support the position and whether the evidence can be checked by the reader.

materials.title: Reading: Two Views on Graffiti
materials.content:
## Expository Text 1: Why Should Graffiti be Considered Art?

In this article, I will explain why graffiti is art, and I will explain how graffiti is essential in our culture. There are some reasons why graffiti shows us the potential that life has to offer.

First, graffiti enables the public to see something they may have never seen before. It connects them to the artist, and the artist gets to know that their work is loved and affects those who see it. They can take a simple old building or any piece of art on the side of a building and turn it into a masterpiece by putting their mark on it. The artists who paint graffiti have made this art form what it is today. Graffiti artists can change the meaning of what they are drawing to the public.

Second, graffiti has the power to affect people positively. The people who create it are expressing themselves. They are expressing their artistic abilities and their voices through a canvas. Their voices are the voices of our future. You can tell the quality of a person's painting by the audience that they are drawing. People will stand and watch you paint for hours. Many times, they will stand and look, never once moving from their spots. People will then tell you how much they like it and share their thoughts and opinions. The artists are no longer making art for themselves.

The last reason why graffiti is an art is because of its uniqueness. Graffiti can be made with many different materials, but its most common form is made by applying paint to a building's wall. Graffiti is made by someone utterly other than the artist, which means no two pieces are the same. Graffiti is a form of expression because it gives the reader or viewer the chance to see something different from their everyday life. Graffiti art is not meant to be understood by everyone, but everyone is meant to be appreciated.

Thus, as part of the existing society, every person must strive to educate themselves of the origins of graffiti and how it has evolved to this very day. A stock of knowledge doesn't hurt; instead, it is a door that leads to understanding and more positivity.

Adapted from: https://theartbay.com/why-should-graffiti-be-considered-art/ (Retrieved March 5, 2022)

## Expository Text 2: Graffiti is Always Vandalism

Anyone who glorifies graffiti needs to answer one question: If your home were tagged during the night without your consent, would you welcome the new addition to your décor or would you immediately call a painter, if not the police?

First of all, graffiti is something that one celebrates, if one is juvenile enough to do so, when it shows up on someone else's property but never on one's own. No institution that has celebrated graffiti in recent years — like the Museum of Contemporary Art in Los Angeles or the Museum of the City of New York — would allow its own premises to be defaced for even one minute.

Next, the question \"When does graffiti become art?\" is meaningless. Graffiti is always vandalism. By definition, it is committed without permission on another person's property, in an adolescent display of entitlement. Whether particular viewers find any given piece of graffiti artistically compelling is irrelevant. Graffiti's most salient characteristic is that it is a crime.

Furthermore, John Lindsay, the progressive New York politician who served as mayor from 1966 to 1973, declared war on graffiti in 1972. He understood that graffiti signaled that informal social controls and law enforcement had broken down in New York's public spaces, making them vulnerable to even greater levels of disorder and law-breaking. A 2008 study from the Netherlands has shown that physical disorder and vandalism have a contagious effect, confirming the \"broken windows theory.\"

In conclusion, there is nothing \"progressive\" about allowing public amenities to be defaced by graffiti; anyone who can avoid a graffiti-bombed park or commercial thoroughfare will do so, since tagging shows that an area is dominated by vandals who may be involved in other crimes as well.

Adapted from: https://www.nytimes.com/roomfordebate/2014/07/11/when-does-graffiti-become-art/graffiti-is-always-vandalism (Retrieved March 6, 2022)

### Which text says it?

### Compare the two texts

| Aspect | Expository Text 1 | Expository Text 2 |
|---|---|---|
| What is the author claiming? | Graffiti is art and is essential in our culture. | Graffiti is always vandalism. |
| What reasons support the claim? | It shows the public something new, affects people positively, and is unique. | It is done without consent, is celebrated only on other people's property, and signals social disorder. |
| What evidence is included? | Artists turn old buildings into masterpieces; audiences watch for hours; no two pieces are the same. | Museums protect their own premises; John Lindsay declared war on graffiti; a 2008 Dutch study on disorder. |
| What is the closing? | People must educate themselves about the origins of graffiti. | Nothing progressive about defacing public amenities; tagging signals vandals and other crimes. |

materials.title: Writing and Responding to Graffiti
materials.content:
## Plan your expository text

Think about your position regarding graffiti, then explain your stance. Consult the list of reasons you have collected: graffiti can decorate a community in some people's eyes, while others say graffiti makes an area look run-down. Write your draft in an expository writing organizer.

| Part of the organizer | What to write |
|---|---|
| Introduction | An interesting opening statement and the main issue |
| Argument 1 | One reason with facts or evidence |
| Argument 2 | A second reason with facts or evidence |
| Argument 3 | A third reason with facts or evidence |
| Conclusion | A closing that restates the position and ties the details together |

### Self and peer review checklist

| Aspect | Question |
|---|---|
| Opening | Does my writing start with an interesting statement to attract readers' attention? |
| Issue | Is the main issue at the beginning of the essay? |
| Structure | Are there at least three parts: introduction, arguments, and conclusion? |
| Evidence | Are facts provided to support the arguments? |
| Word choice | Does the writing avoid repeating the same words over and over? |
| Mechanics | Are capitalisation, punctuation, and spelling correct? |
| Conclusion | Does the conclusion wrap the passage as a whole? |
| Length | Does the writing consist of 200 to 250 words? |

After revision, make the necessary changes based on your classmate's suggestions, turn in your work for a final review by your teacher, and publish it in the media of your choice.

### Public survey project

A group project can measure what the public thinks about graffiti. First, plan: pinpoint your target demographic, identify the number of respondents you need, and pick the right moment to conduct the survey. Second, create the survey and decide how it will be designed. Third, conduct it by sending the survey to the targeted respondents. Fourth, present the result in a short expository essay that talks about public opinion about graffiti, including the survey result as facts to support your arguments.

- A good survey question is open-ended rather than a multiple choice.
- The question is phrased without bias, so respondents are not pushed to one answer.
- The survey is turned in on time and presented neatly.

### Responding with PMI

Record the graffiti you can find in your neighbourhood with photographs: general views of the area and building, details of the graffiti and the surface condition, a scale such as a newspaper or water bottle, and any paint canisters or stencils left near the scene. Then respond to the graffiti in pairs using the Plus, Minus, Interesting (PMI) strategy to consider the question \"Is graffiti art or vandalism?\"

- Words that may help: beautiful, expressive, eyesore, disturbing, destructive, costly.
- Relate your response to the values of Profil Pelajar Pancasila.
- If \"kreatif\" is chosen, graffiti may be seen mainly as art.
- If civic responsibility is the main consideration, graffiti may be seen as vandalism.

questions.explanation: Teks 2 menyatakan penilaian estetis pengamat \"is irrelevant\" karena statusnya tetap pelanggaran hukum.

questions.question: Which statement from Text 1 is an opinion rather than a verifiable fact?

options.text: Graffiti has the power to affect people positively.
John Lindsay served as mayor from 1966 to 1973.
A 2008 study came from the Netherlands.
Graffiti is often made by applying paint to a building's wall.

questions.explanation: \"Has the power to affect people positively\" adalah penilaian penulis, bukan data yang dapat diperiksa.

questions.question: What does \"A stock of knowledge doesn't hurt\" mean in Text 1's closing?

options.text: Learning about graffiti's origins leads to understanding and positivity.
Graffiti should be taught only to artists.

questions.explanation: Kalimat itu berarti pengetahuan tambahan tidak merugikan, tetapi membuka jalan menuju pemahaman.

questions.question: Why does Text 2 call the question \"When does graffiti become art?\" meaningless?

options.text: Because by definition graffiti is committed without permission, so it is always vandalism.
Because no one has ever asked it before.
Because museums refuse to answer it.

questions.explanation: Bagi penulis Teks 2, definisi graffiti sudah mengandung unsur tanpa izin, sehingga pertanyaan itu tidak relevan.

questions.question: What is the function of \"First\", \"Second\", and \"The last reason\" in Text 1?

options.text: To organise the arguments so readers can follow them
To show the events happened in the past
To give instructions to the reader

questions.explanation: Penanda urutan membantu pembaca mengikuti rangkaian argumen secara sistematis.

questions.question: Which evidence does Text 2 use to support its position?

options.text: Museum practice, John Lindsay's policy, and a 2008 Dutch study
A interview with a graffiti artist

questions.explanation: Teks 2 menguatkan argumennya dengan praktik museum, kebijakan Lindsay, dan studi Belanda 2008.

questions.question: What does \"contagious effect\" imply in Text 2?

options.text: Visible disorder spreads and invites more law-breaking.
Vandalism is limited to one building.

questions.explanation: Menular berarti kekacauan yang dibiarkan cenderung menular ke pelanggaran lain.

questions.question: How do the two texts differ in their closing?

options.text: Text 1 calls readers to educate themselves; Text 2 concludes that graffiti defaces public amenities.
Text 1 asks readers to call the police; Text 2 invites readers to paint.
Both texts close with survey data.
Both texts close by describing a museum.

questions.explanation: Teks 1 menutup dengan ajakan belajar tentang asal-usul graffiti; Teks 2 menutup dengan simpulan bahwa graffiti merusak fasilitas publik.

questions.question: A classmate writes, \"Graffiti is bad because I do not like it.\" What is the best revision for an analytical exposition?

options.text: Replace the personal dislike with a reason and evidence, such as the cost of cleaning public property.
Repeat \"I do not like it\" three times for emphasis.
Add more adjectives without any facts.
Delete the conclusion and keep the opinion.

questions.explanation: Analytical exposition membutuhkan alasan dan bukti yang dapat diperiksa, bukan sekadar selera pribadi.

questions.question: Which are features of an analytical exposition? Choose all that apply.

options.text: A series of past events told in time order

questions.explanation: Tiga ciri pertama adalah struktur analytical exposition; rangkaian peristiwa masa lalu milik recount.

questions.question: Arrange the process of writing an expository text about graffiti.

options.text: Write the draft and do a review

questions.explanation: Posisi → alasan dan bukti → organizer → draft dan tinjauan → revisi dan publikasi.
